detailed_summary: This paper reports a field demonstration of a dual-function, common-aperture free-space optical (FSO) system that simultaneously performs decoy-state BB84 quantum key distribution (QKD) at 803 nm and bidirectional classical laser communication at 640/660 nm over a 10.31 km terrestrial link between a mobile platform and a stationary ground station. The classical link uses Manchester-coded on-off keying (MC-OOK) at 10 MHz, achieving a packet error rate of ~0.4% (estimated BER 3.13×10⁻⁵) with hardware-based self-synchronization and error-packet retransmission. The QKD system achieved an average QBER of 2.512% and an average secret key rate of 644 bps using rate-adaptive LDPC codes. Real-time AES-256 encrypted image transmission was executed over the co-aligned classical channel using the distilled keys, demonstrating a self-contained, jam-resistant mobile quantum optical network. The authors claim this is the first field demonstration of a fully integrated common-aperture architecture where a co-propagating classical optical link simultaneously performs full QKD post-processing and encrypted payload transmission over a 10 km atmospheric channel.
key_contributions: First field demonstration of a common-aperture free-space optical system integrating decoy-state BB84 QKD at 803 nm with bidirectional classical laser communication at 640/660 nm over a 10.31 km terrestrial link from a mobile platform.

Achieved simultaneous QKD post-processing and encrypted payload transmission over the same atmospheric channel, with an average QBER of 2.512% and secret key rate of 644 bps using rate-adaptive LDPC codes.
Demonstrated classical communication with MC-OOK at 10 MHz, achieving a packet error rate of ~0.4% (BER 3.13×10⁻⁵) via hardware-based self-synchronization and error-packet retransmission.
Executed real-time AES-256 encrypted image transmission using distilled QKD keys over the co-aligned classical optical channel, proving feasibility of a self-contained mobile quantum optical network.
Showcased a jam-resistant architecture by co-propagating classical and quantum signals through a single aperture, reducing size, weight, and power (SWaP) for mobile platforms.
methodology_analysis: The system employs a common-aperture design to co-propagate quantum and classical signals, minimizing alignment complexity and SWaP. The QKD implementation uses the decoy-state BB84 protocol at 803 nm, with rate-adaptive LDPC codes for error correction. The classical link uses Manchester-coded on-off keying (MC-OOK) at 10 MHz, which provides DC balance and clock recovery, enabling hardware-based self-synchronization. Error-packet retransmission is implemented to ensure reliable data transfer. The field link spans 10.31 km between a mobile platform and a stationary ground station, introducing realistic atmospheric turbulence and loss. The authors likely employ wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) to separate the quantum and classical channels, though the paper does not detail the filtering scheme. The post-processing includes key distillation and AES-256 encryption for image transmission, demonstrating end-to-end integration.
results_analysis: The QKD system achieved an average QBER of 2.512%, which is below the typical 11% security threshold for BB84, and an average secret key rate of 644 bps. The classical link achieved a packet error rate of ~0.4% (BER 3.13×10⁻⁵) at 10 MHz MC-OOK, with hardware-based self-synchronization and retransmission ensuring reliability. The secret key rate is relatively low but sufficient for AES-256 key refresh and encrypted image transmission. The QBER is consistent with typical free-space QKD over ~10 km, though the secret key rate is modest compared to fiber-based systems. The simultaneous operation demonstrates that classical and quantum signals can coexist in a common aperture without significant crosstalk, though the paper does not provide detailed crosstalk measurements.
strengths: First field demonstration of a fully integrated common-aperture QKD and classical communication system over a 10 km atmospheric link, showcasing practical integration for mobile platforms.
Real-time AES-256 encrypted image transmission using distilled QKD keys, proving end-to-end security functionality.
Use of rate-adaptive LDPC codes and hardware-based self-synchronization enhances robustness and efficiency in a turbulent channel.
Bidirectional classical link with error-packet retransmission ensures reliable data transfer, addressing atmospheric fading.
limitations: The secret key rate of 644 bps is relatively low for high-bandwidth applications, limiting practical throughput.
The paper lacks detailed analysis of crosstalk between classical and quantum channels, which is critical for common-aperture systems.
The mobile platform's movement and its impact on link stability and QKD performance are not thoroughly quantified.
connections_to_research: This work directly connects to quantum physics and quantum information science, particularly in the areas of quantum key distribution, free-space quantum communication, and integrated quantum-classical photonic systems. It demonstrates the practical deployment of decoy-state BB84 in a realistic field setting, addressing challenges such as atmospheric turbulence, co-propagation crosstalk, and mobile platform integration. The results are relevant to researchers interested in quantum networks, secure communication, and the coexistence of quantum and classical signals in shared optical channels.
overall_assessment: The paper presents a significant advancement in field-deployed quantum communication by demonstrating a fully integrated common-aperture system that simultaneously performs QKD and classical communication over a 10 km link. The novelty lies in the successful co-propagation and real-time encrypted transmission, though the secret key rate is modest and crosstalk analysis is limited. The work is of high quality for a field demonstration and provides a foundation for mobile quantum optical networks, but further optimization and detailed characterization are needed for practical deployment.
